q: What is the product when aniline is treated with NaNO<sub>2</sub> and aqueous HCl at 0–5 °C?
h: HNO<sub>2</sub> in acid generates the nitrosonium ion, NO<sup>+</sup>. A primary arylamine has two N–H bonds to lose.
w: NaNO2 and HCl form HNO2, which gives NO+. The NH2 nitrogen attacks NO+ to give an N-nitrosamine, which tautomerizes and loses water to form the benzenediazonium ion, Ar–N≡N+ (here as its chloride). Aryl diazonium salts are stable enough to use in solution below about 5 °C.
x: Phenol forms only when the diazonium solution is warmed in water; at 0–5 °C the diazonium salt persists.
The N-nitroso compound is the first intermediate for a 1° amine; it loses water to the diazonium ion. Stable N-nitrosamines come from 2° amines.
Nitrous acid does not oxidize the amine nitrogen to a nitro group; it transfers NO<sup>+</sup>.

q: What is the major product when N-methylaniline is treated with NaNO<sub>2</sub> and aqueous HCl at 0 °C?
h: A 2° amine has only one N–H. After NO<sup>+</sup> bonds to nitrogen, can it lose water to form N≡N?
w: The secondary nitrogen attacks NO+ and loses its single N–H proton, giving an N-nitrosamine, Ar(CH3)N–N=O. With no second N–H, it cannot tautomerize and lose water, so no diazonium ion forms; the N-nitrosamine is the stable product (and such compounds are potent carcinogens).
x: Ring C-nitrosation at the para position is typical of 3° arylamines such as N,N-dimethylaniline, which have no N–H.
Forming a diazonium ion requires a 1° amine; this nitrogen would have to lose its methyl group.
Nitrous acid nitrosates (adds N=O); it does not deliver an NO<sub>2</sub> group to nitrogen.

q: What is the final product of the sequence shown?
h: Follow each step in turn: diazotization, a Sandmeyer reaction, then a nitrile reaction under hot aqueous acid.
w: Diazotization converts 4-methylaniline into its diazonium salt. CuCN replaces N2+ with CN (Sandmeyer), giving 4-methylbenzonitrile. Hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile completely, through the amide, to the carboxylic acid: 4-methylbenzoic acid.
x: 4-Methylbenzonitrile is the product after step 2; heating with H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> hydrolyzes the C≡N.
The diazonium group was already replaced by CN in step 2, so no diazonium is left to be converted into a phenol in step 3.
The amide is an intermediate in nitrile hydrolysis; prolonged heating with aqueous acid takes it on to the acid.

1. HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  2. Sn, HCl; then NaOH  3. Br<sub>2</sub> (excess), H<sub>2</sub>O  4. NaNO<sub>2</sub>, HCl, 0 °C  5. CuBr

h: The three Br atoms are meta to each other, yet Br is an o,p-director. Which group could place them, and then be removed without a trace?
w: Bromines that are mutually meta can all be ortho/para to one strongly activating group. Nitration and reduction give aniline; aqueous Br2 brominates every ortho and para position, giving 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Diazotization and then H3PO2 replace N2+ with H, removing the directing group: 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.
x: Bromine directs ortho/para, so successive brominations of benzene give mainly 1,2,4-tribromobenzene, not the 1,3,5 isomer.
CuBr replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> with Br, giving 1,2,3,5-tetrabromobenzene; H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> is needed to replace it with H.
Heating the diazonium salt in water replaces N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> with OH, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

q: Which sequence converts aniline into fluorobenzene?
h: Fluoride is introduced from a non-nucleophilic counterion that the dry diazonium salt carries with it.
w: Adding HBF4 to the diazonium solution precipitates the arenediazonium tetrafluoroborate. Heating the dry salt releases N2 and BF3 and delivers fluoride to the ring (the Balz–Schiemann reaction), giving fluorobenzene. Copper(I) fluoride is not used; Sandmeyer reactions cover Cl, Br and CN.
x: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen, giving benzene.
In hot water, the solvent captures the aryl cation and gives phenol; fluoride ion is a poor nucleophile in water.
CuCl is the Sandmeyer reagent for chlorobenzene, not fluorobenzene.

q: What is the major product of the sequence shown?
h: Sulfuric acid is used instead of HCl in step 1. Which nucleophile is left to capture the aryl group in step 2?
w: Diazotization gives the arenediazonium hydrogen sulfate. On warming in water the diazonium group leaves as N2, and water (the only good nucleophile present; HSO4− is very weak) bonds to the ring carbon. Loss of H+ gives 4-ethylphenol. H2SO4 rather than HCl is used to avoid aryl chloride by-products.
x: Replacement by H needs a reducing agent such as H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>; hot water gives the phenol.
No chloride is present (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> was used), and replacing N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> by Cl efficiently needs CuCl.
Nitrous acid converts a 1° arylamine into a diazonium ion; it does not oxidize the amine to a nitro group.

q: Benzenediazonium chloride is added to phenol in mildly basic solution (pH about 9). What is the major product?
h: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile that attacks only a strongly activated ring. Where does the phenoxide ion direct, and which position is least hindered?
w: At pH 9 some phenol is present as phenoxide, a very strongly activated ring. The terminal nitrogen of the diazonium ion is the electrophile in an electrophilic aromatic substitution, and coupling occurs para to O−, the least hindered activated position, giving 4-hydroxyazobenzene (an azo dye, drawn as the more stable E isomer).
x: Ortho coupling occurs only when the para position is blocked; the bulky electrophile prefers the open para position.
The meta position is not activated by OH or O<sup>−</sup>, so the weakly electrophilic diazonium ion does not attack there.
O-attack to form a diazo ether is not the observed outcome; diazonium ions couple at ring carbon to give the conjugated azo compound.

q: Which arenediazonium ion reacts fastest in azo coupling with N,N-dimethylaniline?
h: In azo coupling the diazonium ion is the electrophile. Which para substituent makes its terminal nitrogen most electron-poor?
w: The rate depends on the electrophilicity of the terminal diazonium nitrogen. A para electron-withdrawing group increases the positive character of that nitrogen, while donors (CH3, and especially OCH3, which donates by resonance into the N≡N+ group) make the ion more stable and less electrophilic. The 4-nitrobenzenediazonium ion couples fastest.
x: A para OCH<sub>3</sub> donates electron density by resonance into the diazonium group, making it the least electrophilic and slowest to couple.
A para methyl group is weakly donating, so this ion is slightly less reactive than the unsubstituted one.
The unsubstituted ion lacks the electron-withdrawing nitro group that raises electrophilicity.

h: Use the nitro group as a meta director first, then turn it into something that can be swapped for Br.
w: The nitro group directs chlorination meta (1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene). Reduction gives 3-chloroaniline, diazotization gives the 3-chlorobenzenediazonium ion, and the Sandmeyer reaction with CuBr replaces N2+ with Br: chlorinate, reduce, diazotize, CuBr.
x: Reducing first makes aniline, an o,p-director that is chlorinated at ortho and para positions (and more than once), so the meta relationship is lost.
Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> brominates ring C–H positions; it does not replace a diazonium group. CuBr is needed.
HBF<sub>4</sub> and heat replace the diazonium group with F, giving 1-chloro-3-fluorobenzene.

q: Imidazole is protonated by one equivalent of HCl. Which atom accepts the proton?
c: N a and N b equally, giving two different cations
h: One nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet; the other's lies in the ring plane.
w: N a (the N–H nitrogen) is pyrrole-like: its lone pair is in a p orbital and is part of the six π electrons. N b is pyridine-like: its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, so N b can bond H+ without disturbing aromaticity. The resulting imidazolium ion is aromatic and symmetric (the charge is shared equally by both N atoms by resonance), which is why imidazole (conjugate-acid pKa about 7.0) is a stronger base than pyridine (5.2).
x: Protonating the N–H nitrogen would use its lone pair, which is part of the aromatic sextet, giving a non-aromatic cation.
Protonating C2 would destroy aromaticity; ring carbon protonation is not competitive with the available nitrogen lone pair.
The two nitrogens are not equivalent in neutral imidazole: only N b has a lone pair outside the π system.

q:
Consider these statements about nitrogen heterocycles.
I. The nitrogen lone pair of pyridine occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane and is not part of the aromatic π system.
II. The nitrogen lone pair of pyrrole occupies a p orbital and is one of the six π electrons of the ring.
III. Pyrrole is protonated mainly on nitrogen, giving an aromatic cation.
IV. Imidazole contains one pyridine-like nitrogen and one pyrrole-like nitrogen.
Which statements are true?
h: For each ring, count π electrons and decide whether the N lone pair is needed to reach six.
w: I is true: pyridine already has six π electrons from its three double bonds, so the lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane. II is true: pyrrole needs the N lone pair in a p orbital to complete its sextet. III is false: N-protonation would remove the lone pair from the π system and destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is a very weak base and protonates (when forced) on C2. IV is true: imidazole has an N–H nitrogen like pyrrole and an N= nitrogen like pyridine. Answer: I, II and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also true: imidazole has one nitrogen of each type.
Statement I is true and statement III is false; protonating pyrrole on N destroys its aromaticity.
Statement III is false: an N-protonated pyrrole is not aromatic, and pyrrole is protonated on carbon.

h: CH<sub>3</sub> directs ortho/para, so a temporary, stronger director para to CH<sub>3</sub> must steer Br meta to CH<sub>3</sub>. Tame it so only one Br adds, then remove it.
w: Nitration and reduction give 4-methylaniline. Acetylation makes the acetamido group, which still outranks CH3 as a director but is mild enough for monobromination; Br enters ortho to NHAc, which is meta to CH3. Hydrolysis frees the amine, and diazotization followed by H3PO2 replaces the nitrogen with H, leaving 3-bromotoluene.
x: Without acetylation, the free NH<sub>2</sub> directs bromine to both of its ortho positions; after deamination the product is 3,5-dibromotoluene.
Hot water replaces the diazonium group with OH, giving 2-bromo-4-methylphenol instead of removing it.

With the nitro group still in place, bromination is directed by CH<sub>3</sub> (ortho to it, which is also meta to NO<sub>2</sub>); after removing the nitrogen the product is 2-bromotoluene, not 3-bromotoluene.

q: 4-(Dimethylamino)pyridine (DMAP, conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> 9.6) is a much stronger base than pyridine (5.2). Which nitrogen is protonated, and why is DMAP so basic?
c: N b; the lone pair on N a donates into the ring by resonance and delocalizes the positive charge of the cation onto N a
N a; it is a 3° alkylamine nitrogen with an undelocalized sp3 lone pair
N a; the pyridine ring withdraws electrons from N b, leaving N a as the only basic site
N b; the dimethylamino group withdraws electron density inductively, which stabilizes the cation
h: Draw the cation from protonating the ring nitrogen. Can the dimethylamino lone pair share the positive charge?
w: N a is attached to an aromatic ring, so its lone pair is conjugated with the ring like that of an aniline; it is not an ordinary alkylamine nitrogen. Protonation at the ring nitrogen N b gives a cation with a resonance form C=N+(CH3)2, in which the positive charge is shared by both nitrogens (an amidinium-like ion). That extra resonance stabilization of the conjugate acid raises the pKa from 5.2 to 9.6.
x: N a is bonded to an aromatic carbon, so its lone pair is delocalized into the ring (like an aniline); protonating it would also lose that conjugation.
The ring nitrogen N b becomes more, not less, electron rich because N a donates into the ring.
The dimethylamino group raises the basicity by resonance donation; an inductive withdrawal would lower it.

q: In which compound is the nitrogen lone pair not part of an aromatic π system?
h: Count the π electrons from double bonds alone. If the ring already has six, the lone pair stays out of the π system.
w: In pyridine the three ring double bonds supply six π electrons; the N lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, perpendicular to the p orbitals. In pyrrole, N-methylpyrrole and indole the five-membered ring has only four π electrons from C=C bonds, so the N lone pair must sit in a p orbital to complete the aromatic sextet.
x: Pyrrole needs the N lone pair to give six π electrons, so it is part of the aromatic system.
N-Methylpyrrole is aromatic in the same way as pyrrole; the methyl group does not change where the lone pair is.
In indole the nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic π system of the five-membered (and the fused ten-electron) ring.

q: An amine C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N gives the mass spectrum shown, with a weak M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 87 and the base peak at m/z 30. Which structure fits?
h: Amines fragment by α-cleavage: the C–C bond next to the C–N carbon breaks, leaving a resonance-stabilized iminium ion. Work out the iminium mass for each candidate.
w: An odd molecular ion (87) fits one nitrogen (nitrogen rule). α-Cleavage of pentan-1-amine breaks the C1–C2 bond and gives CH2=NH2+, m/z 30, the base peak for amines with an unbranched RCH2NH2 group. Each other isomer gives a heavier iminium ion because it carries extra carbon on the α carbon or on nitrogen.
x: Pentan-2-amine loses the propyl radical by α-cleavage to give CH<sub>3</sub>CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 44.
N-Methylbutan-1-amine loses a propyl radical to give CH<sub>2</sub>=NHCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 44.
N,N-Dimethylpropan-1-amine loses an ethyl radical to give CH<sub>2</sub>=N(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, m/z 58.
